1 | INTRODUCTION
International law has long treated human rights law and international 
environmental law as separate fields. However, the problems they 
address significantly overlap and the fields increasingly influence 
one another. In some respects, they are even beginning to merge. 
The Global Pact for the Environment has the potential to be a mile­
stone in this rapidly developing relationship.1
As its name suggests, the Global Pact is quite ambitious; it aspires 
to be nothing less than a new international environmental constitu­
tion. The Pact was drafted by environmental law experts from differ­
ent countries, working under the auspices of the environment 
commission of the Club des Juristes, a French legal think tank. Laurent 
Fabius, the president of the French Conseil Constitutionnel, chaired the 
meeting of the experts in June 2017 at which the text was finalized.2
The most obvious precursor of the Global Pact is the 1992 Rio 
Declaration on Environment and Development, many of whose prin­
ciples the Pact repeats in similar or even identical language.3 However, 
as Yann Aguila and Jorge Viñuales explain, the Pact goes beyond the 
Rio Declaration in significant respects, including by codifying the prin­
ciples in the form of a legally binding instrument, by including some 
new principles, and by providing for a committee of experts to monitor 
compliance and facilitate implementation of the Pact.4
In the fall of 2017, the French government promoted the Pact in 
several forums, including a high-­level side event at the United 
Nations (UN) General Assembly in New York in September. In May 
2018, the General Assembly adopted a resolution entitled ‘Towards 
a Global Pact for the Environment’, which requested the Secretary-­
General to submit a report on gaps in international environmental 
law and environment-­related instruments, and established an open-­
ended working group to consider the report and discuss possible 
options to address such gaps, ‘and, if deemed necessary, the scope, 
parameters and feasibility of an international instrument, with a 
view to making recommendations, which may include the convening 
of an intergovernmental conference to adopt an international instru­
ment, to the Assembly during the first half of 2019’.5
The present article does not attempt to predict what will emerge 
from this process. The final result, if any, may not look much like the

The Global Pact for the Environment has the potential to be a milestone in the rapidly 
developing relationship of human rights and the environment. Most importantly, the 
first article recognizes the right of every person ‘to live in an ecologically sound envir­
onment adequate for their health, well-­being, dignity, culture and fulfilment’. This 
article provides context for the proposal to recognize the human right to a healthy 
environment. It reviews previous efforts to recognize the human right to a healthy 
environment at the national and international levels; explains how other human 
rights, such as rights to life and health, have been construed to apply to environmen­
tal issues; and describes how recognition of the right in the Global Pact, or in another 
instrument such as a resolution of the United Nations General Assembly, would con­
tribute to the growing field of environmental human rights law.

Global Pact. Even if it does resemble the Pact, it may not attract the 
support necessary to meet the goal of establishing a new framework for 
international environmental protection. Instead, this article highlights 
one aspect of the draft Global Pact that is noteworthy regardless of 
the outcome of the process: the way that this proposal for a new inter­
national environmental constitution reflects and supports the growing 
interdependence of human rights norms and environmental protection.
Although several provisions of the Pact recall human rights prin­
ciples, the most important in this respect is the very first article, 
which would recognize for the first time in a global treaty the right of 
every person ‘to live in an ecologically sound environment adequate 
for their health, well-­being, dignity, culture and fulfilment’.6 This art­
icle places this provision in context and explains its potential signifi­
cance. Specifically, it reviews the previous efforts to recognize the 
human right to a healthy environment at the national and interna­
tional levels; describes how other human rights, such as rights to life 
and health, have been construed to apply to environmental issues; 
and explains how recognition of the right to a healthy environment 
in a new international instrument would contribute to the evolution 
of environmental human rights law.7
2 | RECOGNITION OF THE RIGHT TO A 
HEALTHY ENVIRONMENT
Despite repeated efforts, the UN has never explicitly recognized the 
human right to a healthy environment in a global instrument. The 
seminal human rights texts – the Universal Declaration of Human 
Rights and the two International Covenants on human rights – do 
not include the right, almost certainly because they were adopted by 
the UN General Assembly in 1948 and 1966 respectively, before the 
modern environmental movement began. Early in that movement, 
advocates began to argue that the importance of the environment to 
human wellbeing required recognition of the human right to a 
healthy environment. They nearly achieved their goal in 1972, at the 
first UN environmental conference. The first principle of the 
Stockholm Declaration adopted by the conference states: ‘man has 
the fundamental right to freedom, equality and adequate conditions 
of life, in an environment of a quality that permits a life of dignity and 
well-­being, and he bears a solemn responsibility to protect and im­
prove the environment for present and future generations’.8
However, the UN has never again come so close to explicit recog­
nition of the right. For example, the 1987 report of the World 
Commission on Environment and Development, which brought for­
ward the concept of sustainable development, includes legal prin­
ciples drafted by an experts group, the first of which declares: ‘all 
human beings have the fundamental right to an environment ad­
equate for their health and well-­being’.9 Rather than adopt this lan­
guage, the 1992 Rio Declaration states only: ‘Human beings are at 
the centre of concerns for sustainable development. They are en­
titled to a healthy and productive life in harmony with nature.’10
In the UN human rights bodies, the most sustained attention to 
the right came in the early 1990s. In 1990, the Sub-­commission on 
Prevention of Discrimination and Protection of Minorities, a body of 
independent experts reporting to the Human Rights Commission, 
the principal UN intergovernmental human rights body at the time, 
appointed Fatma Zohra Ksentini as its special rapporteur on human 
rights and the environment. Her final report, presented in 1994, in­
cluded draft principles on human rights and the environment, which 
state that everyone has ‘the right to a secure, healthy and ecologic­
ally sound environment’ and list a number of related rights, including 
rights to freedom from pollution, to protection and preservation of 
the air, soil, water, sea-­ice, flora and fauna, to safe and healthy food 
and water, and to information concerning the environment.11 The 
Human Rights Commission considered the report, but it did not 
adopt or endorse the draft principles or appoint a special rapporteur 
itself.
In contrast to the lack of action at the UN, many regional agree­
ments and national laws have incorporated the right to a healthy en­
vironment. The first international agreement to recognize the right 
was the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, adopted in 
1981, which states that ‘all peoples shall have the right to a general 
satisfactory environment favourable to their development’.12 Seven 
years later, the San Salvador Protocol to the American Convention 
on Human Rights became the first treaty to characterize the right as 
an individual rather than a collective right, stating simply that ‘every­
one shall have the right to live in a healthy environment’.13 In 2003, 
the African Union adopted the Maputo Protocol to the African 
Charter, which states that women shall have ‘the right to live in a 
healthy and sustainable environment’ and ‘the right to fully enjoy 
their right to sustainable development’.14 The Arab Charter on

Human Rights of 2004 includes the right to a healthy environment as 
part of the right to an adequate standard of living that ensures well­
being and a decent life, as does the Human Rights Declaration  
adopted by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in 2012.15
Alone among the regional human rights systems, the European 
Convention on Human Rights (setting out civil and political rights) 
and the European Social Charter (identifying economic, social and 
cultural rights) do not include the right to a healthy environment. 
However, the European Committee of Social Rights, which has the 
non-­binding authority to oversee compliance with the Social Charter, 
has interpreted the right to protection of health in Article 11 of the 
Charter to include an implicit right to a healthy environment.16
Although they are not usually considered human rights agree­
ments, two regional agreements on procedural rights of access to 
information, public participation and remedies in environmental 
matters also refer to the human right to a healthy environment. The 
Aarhus Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in 
Decision-­making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters, 
adopted in 1998 under the auspices of the UN Economic Commission 
for Europe, states as its objective that the parties shall guarantee 
these rights of access ‘[i]n order to contribute to the protection of 
the right of every person of present and future generations to live in 
an environment adequate to his or her health and well-­being’.17 
Similarly, the Regional Agreement on Access to Information, Public 
Participation and Justice in Environmental Matters in Latin America 
and the Caribbean (known as the Escazú Agreement), which opened 
for signature in 2018, states that one of its objectives is ‘contributing 
to the protection of the right of every person of present and future 
generations to live in a healthy environment and to sustainable de­
velopment’.18 It goes further than the Aarhus Convention by also 
requiring that each of its parties ‘guarantee the right of every person 
to live in a healthy environment’.19
At the national level, Portugal became the first country to adopt 
a constitutional ‘right to a healthy and ecologically balanced human 
environment’ in 1976. The number of countries explicitly recognizing 
the right in national constitutions has grown steadily and is now at 
least 100.20 About two-­thirds of these constitutions refer to a 
healthy environment; alternative formulations include rights to a 
clean, safe, favourable, wholesome or ecologically balanced environ­
ment. Many other States have enacted legislation that refers to the 
right to a healthy environment. Some States, including India and 
Pakistan, have interpreted other rights, such as the right to life, to 
incorporate the right to a healthy environment.21
In all, more than 150 States have recognized the right through 
regional agreements, national constitutions, or other national laws 
or court decisions. The right could thus be said to have achieved 
near-­global support even in the absence of a global instrument expli­
citly recognizing it, although the remaining hold-­outs include some 
powerful, populous countries, notably China, Japan and the United 
States, as well as Australia and Canada.
Although in some States the right may be merely aspirational or 
symbolic, the agencies and courts of many others regularly rely on 
the right to authorize or require stronger environmental measures.22 
At the international level, however, regional tribunals and other  
bodies have only occasionally cited the right. Instead, as the next 
section explains, international human rights bodies have contributed 
to the growing body of environmental human rights law by applying 
more well-­established human rights to environmental issues.
3 | INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL 
HUMAN RIGHTS LAW
For nearly 25 years, international human rights bodies have ‘greened’ 
human rights law by holding that environmental harm implicates a 
very wide variety of human rights, including the rights to life, health 
and property. Through decisions and statements by regional human 
rights tribunals and commissions, UN human rights treaty bodies, 
special rapporteurs and others, human rights law has developed an 
environmental jurisprudence.
To examine and report on this growing field, the UN Human 
Rights Council, which replaced the Human Rights Commission in 
2006, decided in 2012 to appoint an independent expert with a 
mandate to study the human rights obligations relating to the enjoy­
ment of a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment.23 Over 
much of the next two years, the independent expert conducted con­
sultations around the world and, with the assistance of many lawyers 
and academics, researched the decisions and statements of human 
rights tribunals and other international bodies on environmental 
matters. Specifically, this ‘mapping project’ examined: (i) UN human 
rights bodies and mechanisms, including resolutions adopted by the 
General Assembly and Human Rights Council, and reports of special 
rapporteurs and other mandate-­holders appointed by the Council; 
(ii) global human rights treaties, as interpreted by the treaty bodies 
given authority to oversee compliance with them; (iii) regional human

rights systems, including decisions of regional human rights courts 
and commissions; and (iv) international environmental instruments.
The independent expert published a series of 14 reports, each 
describing what one source or set of sources had said about environ­
mental issues.24 He summarized the conclusions of these reports to 
the Human Rights Council in an overall mapping report, published in 
December 2013 and presented to the Council in March 2014.25
The sources reviewed overwhelmingly agreed that environmen­
tal harm threatens a vast range of human rights, including rights to 
life, health, property, home and family life, food, water, culture and 
self-­determination.26 They also agreed that States have obligations 
to protect human rights from interference from environmental harm. 
Despite differences in the language of the treaties and in the specific 
rights that the bodies were interpreting, the sources reached re­
markably similar conclusions about the nature of these obligations. 
They stated that in order to protect against environmental harm, 
States have procedural obligations, including duties to assess envir­
onmental impacts and make environmental information public, to 
facilitate public participation in environmental decision making and 
to provide access to effective remedies.27 States also have substan­
tive duties to adopt and implement legal frameworks to protect 
against environmental harm, including by regulating corporations 
and other private actors.28 Finally, they have duties to protect 
against discrimination in environmental law and policy, and to take 
additional steps to protect those who are at particular risk from en­
vironmental harm.29
In 2015, the Council renewed the mandate for another three 
years, changed the title of the mandate-­holder to ‘special rappor­
teur’, and requested that he promote and report on the realization of 
human rights obligations relating to the enjoyment of a safe, clean, 
healthy and sustainable environment, disseminate his findings, and 
identify challenges and obstacles to the full realization of such obli­
gations.30 In accordance with that charge, the special rapporteur 
sought, among other things, to develop guidance that clearly de­
scribes the human rights norms of special relevance to the 
environment.
To that end, and after consultation with governments, civil society 
organizations and other stakeholders, he prepared Framework 
Principles on Human Rights and the Environment, which he presented 
to the Council in March 2018.31 The 16 Framework Principles and 
their accompanying commentary do not purport to create new obliga­
tions; rather, they provide a restatement of existing obligations of 
States under human rights law as they relate to the environment.32
The Principles include specific procedural obligations, such as 
the duties of States to respect and protect the rights to freedom of 
expression, association and peaceful assembly in relation to environ­
mental matters, provide for environmental education and public 
awareness, provide public access to environmental information, re­
quire prior assessment of the possible environmental and human 
rights impacts of proposed projects and policies, provide for and fa­
cilitate public participation in decision making related to the environ­
ment, and provide for access to effective remedies for violations of 
human rights and domestic laws relating to the environment.33
The Principles also set out human rights obligations relating to 
substantive standards. Human rights bodies have made clear that 
while environmental standards should ideally be set and implemented 
at levels that would prevent all environmental harm from human 
sources, States do have discretion, in light of limited resources, to seek 
to achieve progressively the full realization of economic, social and 
cultural rights, including in the environmental context.34 However, this 
discretion is not unlimited. For example, the establishment and imple­
mentation of environmental standards must always comply with obli­
gations of non-­discrimination, and there is a strong presumption 
against retrogressive measures. Other relevant factors include 
whether the standards take into account relevant international stand­
ards, such as those promulgated by the World Health Organization. In 
short, States must not strike an unjustifiable or unreasonable balance 
between environmental protection and other social goals.35
Governments must comply with their legal standards once  
adopted, and monitor and effectively enforce compliance by corpor­
ations and other private actors. In accordance with the Guiding 
Principles on Business and Human Rights endorsed by the Human 
Rights Council in 2011, corporations also have the direct responsibility 
to respect human rights, which includes the responsibility to avoid 
causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts through  
environmental harm and to address such impacts when they occur.36
States also have obligations to cooperate with one another to 
address transboundary and global threats to human rights, such as 
climate change and the global loss of biological diversity. Again, once 
such cooperation has resulted in standards and commitments, such 
as those in multilateral environmental agreements, States have obli­
gations under international law to comply with the standards and 
commitments in good faith.37
States must ensure that their actions relating to the environment 
do not discriminate, and they must protect against environmental

also obligated to take special care to respect, protect and fulfil the 
rights of those who are most at risk from environmental harm, in­
cluding indigenous peoples.39
In presenting the Framework Principles to the Council, the spe­
cial rapporteur made clear that:
[w]hile many of the obligations described in the frame-
work principles and commentary are based directly on 
treaties or binding decisions from human rights tribunals, 
others draw on statements of human rights bodies that 
have the authority to interpret human rights law but not 
necessarily to issue binding decisions. The coherence of 
these interpretations, however, is strong evidence of the 
converging trends towards greater uniformity and cer-
tainty in the understanding of human rights obligations 
relating to the environment. These trends are further 
supported by State practice, including in international 
environmental instruments and before human rights 
bodies.40
The special rapporteur therefore urged States to accept the 
Principles as reflecting actual or emerging international human rights 
law.
He also urged the Council to consider supporting the recognition 
by the UN of the human right to a healthy environment. Noting that 
the great majority of countries in the world had already incorporated 
the right into law, he stated that:
recognition of the right has proved to have real advan-
tages. It has raised the profile and importance of environ-
mental protection and provided a basis for the enactment 
of stronger environmental laws. When applied by the ju-
diciary, it has helped to provide a safety net to protect 
against gaps in statutory laws and created opportunities 
for better access to justice.41
He also noted that because of the clarification of the environmental 
aspects of human rights law, as reflected in the Framework Principles,
the ‘human right to a healthy environment’ is not an 
empty vessel waiting to be filled; on the contrary, its con-
tent has already been clarified, through recognition by 
human rights authorities that a safe, clean, healthy and 
sustainable environment is necessary for the full 
enjoyment of the human rights to life, health, food, water, 
housing and so forth.42
In response to the report, the Council did not formally endorse 
the principles or the call for recognition of the right. However, it did 
adopt a resolution by consensus that took note with appreciation of 
the report presenting the Principles, renewed the mandate for an­
other three years and requested the new mandate-­holder to report 
annually not just to the Human Rights Council, as in the past, but also 
to the General Assembly.43
4 | HAS THE TIME COME FOR THE 
UNITED NATIONS TO RECOGNIZE THE 
RIGHT TO A HEALTHY ENVIRONMENT?
The first report of the UN special rapporteur on human rights and the 
environment to the UN General Assembly repeats the call for the UN 
to recognize the right to a healthy environment.44 The report de­
scribes three possible vehicles for such recognition: (i) the General 
Assembly could recognize the right through a resolution, as it recog­
nized the rights to water and sanitation in 2010; (ii) the parties to one 
of the global human rights treaties, such as the International Covenant 
on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, could adopt a protocol incorp­
orating the right; and (iii) the UN could adopt a new treaty including 
the right, such as the Global Pact.45 The report notes the decision by 
the General Assembly to establish an ad hoc open-­ended working 
group to discuss possible options to address gaps in international  
environmental law and environment-­related instruments, and states that 
any instrument resulting from this process ‘certainly could and should 
include recognition of the human right to a healthy environment’.46
This section first describes the possible advantages of recogni­
tion of the human right to a healthy environment, as detailed in the 
report of the special rapporteur, and then discusses the potential 
role of the Global Pact in particular.
4.1 | Possible benefits of recognition of the human 
right to a healthy environment
The report to the General Assembly outlines several benefits of 
global recognition of the human right to a healthy environment.

First, recognition
 would raise awareness of and reinforce the understand-
ing that human rights norms require protection of the 
environment and that environmental protection depends 
on the exercise of human rights. It would highlight that 
environmental protection must be assigned the same 
level of importance as other interests that are fundamen-
tal to human dignity, equality and freedom.47
Second, it would crystallize and integrate the human rights norms 
relating to the environment, helping to ensure that they ‘continue to 
develop in a coherent, consistent and integrated manner’.48 Usually 
human rights law first recognizes a right in a declaration or treaty, then 
elaborates its corresponding duties over time through implementation 
and interpretation by States and monitoring bodies. In this case, the 
duties have already been elaborated even without a globally recog­
nized right. The absence of a universally acknowledged right has not 
prevented the evolution of environmental human rights law, as the pre­
vious section explains, but the presence of the right would provide a 
kind of capstone to that body of law, giving it a more unified and inte­
grated presence. In the words of Marcos Orellana, ‘[t]he normative 
content of human rights in respect of the environment would thus no 
longer be dispersed or fragmented across a range of rights, but would 
come together under a single normative frame’.49
Third, the report points out that levels of environmental protec­
tion are too often viewed in the aggregate, with insufficient attention 
paid to the disproportionate effects of environmental harm on those 
who are most vulnerable or already marginalized. Recognition of the 
human right to a healthy environment would help to place greater 
attention on those who are most at risk from environmental degrada­
tion, including women, children, persons living in poverty, members 
of indigenous peoples and traditional communities, older persons, 
persons with disabilities, minorities and displaced persons.50
Fourth, the report points to the experience with the right at the 
national level, where it has ‘raised the profile and importance of envir­
onmental protection and provided a basis for the enactment of stron­
ger environmental laws, standards, regulations and policies’.51 In 
particular, the procedural components of the right (including access to 
information, participation and effective remedies) have empowered 
individuals and communities to advocate for and secure better envir­
onmental protection.52 The report states that ‘[t]he ultimate test in 
evaluating the right to a healthy environment is whether it contributes 
to healthier people and healthier ecosystems’.53 It cites empirical  
studies that have concluded, among other things, that:
[i] nations with the right to a healthy environment in their 
constitutions have smaller ecological footprints, rank higher 
on comprehensive indices of environmental indicators, are 
more likely to ratify international environmental agreements 
and have made faster progress in reducing emissions of sul-
phur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and greenhouse gases than 
nations without such provisions … [ii] constitutional environ-
mental rights have a positive causal influence on environ-
mental performance … [and iii] constitutional environmental 
rights are positively related to increases in the proportion of 
populations with access to safe drinking water.54
The General Assembly has historically been careful not to pro­
claim new human rights without careful review. In 1986, it adopted 
guidelines for recognition of new human rights instruments, indicat­
ing that they should:
(i)  Be consistent with the existing body of international 
human rights law;
(ii) Be of fundamental character and derive from the in-
herent dignity and worth of the human person;
(iii) Be sufficiently precise to give rise to identifiable and 
practical rights and obligations;
(iv) Provide, where appropriate, realistic and effective 
implementation machinery, including reporting sys-
tems; [and]
(v) Attract broad international support.55 
Marcos Orellana has persuasively argued that the right to a healthy 
environment satisfies these requirements. He notes that the connection 
between the environment and human dignity has been recognized by 
the UN at least since the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, and the applica­
tion of human rights law to environmental issues (as described in the pre­
vious section) demonstrates that the right is consistent with the existing 
body of human rights law and ‘sufficiently precise to give rise to identifi­
able and practical rights and obligations’. As explained in Section 2, 
‘broad international support’ is shown by the fact that the great majority 
of UN member States have already recognized the right in national law, 
regional agreements or both. With respect to implementation, Orellana 
notes that the question of whether existing machinery is effective ‘re­
mains open for virtually all human rights’.56 However, implementation of 
the human right to a healthy environment at the national level is already 
taking place in many countries, and international mechanisms such as the

4.2 | Human rights and the environment in the 
Global Pact
The benefits of global recognition of the human right to a healthy 
environment that are described above do not depend on its inclusion 
in a binding treaty. Indeed, seeking recognition in a resolution of the 
General Assembly has some important advantages over pursuing a 
treaty. A resolution would almost certainly take less time, since it 
would be viewed by States as less legally significant and therefore 
more politically palatable. For the same reasons, it might capture a 
broader array of State support.59 Any attempt to amend the 
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, or 
include an additional protocol, to include an explicit environmental 
right could take years for approval, and many more years for accept­
ance by nearly all of the members of the UN.
However, including the right in a treaty such as the Global Pact 
does have certain advantages over a resolution. The most obvious, 
of course, is that the treaty would have a binding effect on its part­ies. 
More specifically, including the human right to a healthy envir­onment 
in an ‘environmental’ treaty could strengthen the growing ties be­
tween human rights norms and environmental principles.60
Many of the provisions of the Global Pact echo well-­known en­
vironmental principles included in the Rio Declaration. For example, 
the reference to precaution in Article 6 follows the language of Rio 
Principle 15; Articles 9–11 on rights of access to information, partici­
pation and remedy expand on the language of Rio Principle 10; the 
reference to environmental impact assessment in Article 5 is similar 
to Rio Principle 17; Article 15, calling for the adoption of effective 
enforcement laws, resembles Rio Principle 11; and Article 18, like 
Rio Principle 7, urges international cooperation.
All of these norms also have links to human rights law. As noted 
above, the rights of information, participation and remedy have been 
applied by human rights bodies in environmental cases, and they are 
included in the Framework Principles on Human Rights and the 
Environment described in the previous section. Another Framework 
Principle requires environmental and social impact assessment;  
others require States to adopt and enforce effective environmental 
laws; yet another addresses international cooperation.61 And human 
rights bodies have cited the precautionary principle as one of the 
factors they weigh in assessing whether States have satisfied human 
rights norms in their substantive environmental standards.62
However, with the exception of the rights of information, par­
ticipation and remedy in Articles 9–11, the Global Pact does not ex­
press its norms as following from or implicating rights of individuals. 
Including the human right to a healthy environment as the first art­
icle of the Pact would help to place the remaining provisions in that 
context. Doing so would make it easier to read the Pact not simply as 
an international environmental agreement, but also as an agreement 
drawing on and incorporating human rights norms. Indeed, all of its 
provisions could be considered as aspects of, or at least related to, 
the fundamental human right to a healthy environment. Although 
precedence does not always imply priority, the first article of the 
Pact does seem to be the most important, because it would establish 
the lens through which the remainder of the Pact would be seen. As 
a result, the article could help to elevate the other provisions into 
statements not just of preference and obligation, but of right, and 
of right not just of States vis-à-vis one another, but of rights held by 
human beings against States.
Infusing international environmental norms with human rights 
in this way would help to re-­orient international environmental 
law from its traditional State-­centric focus, according to which its 
obligations are owed only by States to other States. Human rights 
norms make clear that States owe obligations not only to one an­
other, but also, and more importantly, to individuals, who therefore 
should have access to compliance mechanisms to ensure that the 
obligations are being met. A human rights approach therefore helps 
to support stronger compliance mechanisms open to the public, as 
well as calls for new agreements on procedural access rights, such 
as the Aarhus Convention and the Escazú Agreement, and even for 
a global Principle 10 agreement. Relatedly, a human rights approach 
can help to re-­orient international environmental law from its trad­
itional focus on transboundary harm. Recognition that environmen­
tal harm implicates human rights even if the harm does not cross an 
international border opens the door to consideration of sustainable 
development in terms of binding human rights obligations, not just 
non-­binding political declarations.
At the same time, experience with human rights norms warns 
against trying to set out so-­called ‘human duties’ in international in­
struments, as Article 2 of the Pact does. There is a long history in 
human rights law of efforts to define duties on individuals. Although 
reviewing that history is beyond the scope of this article, it is clear 
that while such efforts may seem to contribute to a sense of com­
mon effort at best, and appear anodyne at worse, in practice they 
have often been Trojan horses designed to provide excuses for 
States to justify failing to comply with their own obligations.63 The 
Global Pact, or any other agreement that emerges from the UN

5 | CONCLUSION
The infusion of human rights norms into international environmental 
law can help to re-­energize the field, by making clear that environ­
mental protection is vital to human wellbeing, dignity, equality and 
freedom; by supplying standards, including for rights to informa­
tion, public participation and access to justice, that are vital to in­
clusive and robust environmental policymaking; and by opening new  
avenues for individuals and communities to seek effective remedies 
for environmental harm. By recognizing the human right to a healthy 
environment, the Global Pact for the Environment has the potential 
to contribute to a rights-­based approach to environmental protec­
tion. At a minimum, even if the Pact is not adopted, it is another im­
portant sign of the increasing attention to the relationship of human 
rights and environmental norms.
At the same time, it is important to underline that this rapidly 
developing relationship does not depend on the Global Pact for the 
Environment. Regardless of the fate of the Global Pact, the evolution 
of environmental human rights law will continue.
